questions.questionText: Why does the page say tokens are used instead of whole words?
questions.explanation:
The model cannot store every word in the world, but it can build any word from a fixed set of chunks.

(A) Whole words usually make text shorter than tokens do. The real problem is the size of the vocabulary.

(C) Computers store text in many ways. Tokens are a design choice made for the model.

options.optionText: Whole words would make every sentence longer
A fixed set of sub-word chunks can build every word, including new ones
Tokens are the only units a computer can store

questions.questionText: You type `cat`, then `unbelievableness`. What will the tokenizer do?
questions.explanation:
Common words stay whole. Rare or long words are built from smaller chunks, as in the example above.

(A) Common short words usually stay as one token. Only rare or long words get chopped.

(B) The vocabulary is fixed and limited. That is exactly why rare words get split.

options.optionText: Both split into several tokens, since every word gets chopped
Both stay as one token, since the vocabulary is very large
`cat` stays one token, and `unbelievableness` splits into several pieces

questions.questionText: You are building a brainstorming tool that should give varied ideas. Which change to the temperature helps most?
questions.explanation:
A higher temperature flattens the probabilities, so surprising words are picked more often.

(B) Zero gives the most focused, repeatable choice. That is the opposite of varied ideas.

(C) Temperature reshapes the probabilities. It is a real setting, not a cosmetic one.

options.optionText: Raise it, so less likely words get a bigger share
Set it to 0, so the model always picks the top word
Leave it alone, since temperature does not change the choice

questions.questionText: At a temperature of 0.1, what does the probability chart look like?
questions.explanation:
A low temperature lets the top word dominate, which gives focused, repeatable answers.

(A) That is where a very high temperature moves the chart, not a low one.

(C) A low temperature favours the most likely words, not the least likely.

options.optionText: All words get about the same probability
The most likely word takes most of the share, so the answer is focused
The least likely word gets the biggest share

questions.questionText: In "The barista handed me a hot cup of ___", why does "bicycle" fail, even though it is a noun?
questions.explanation:
Grammar alone would accept a noun. The context is what rules out "bicycle".

(A) A cup of ___ needs a noun, and bicycle is a noun. Grammar is not the problem here.

(B) Length is not the issue. The blank is about what fits in a cup.

options.optionText: It is the wrong part of speech, since the blank needs a verb
The sentence is too long for the word to fit
It does not fit the meaning: a cup holds a drink, not a vehicle

questions.questionText: Why does this training need no human labels?
questions.explanation:
The internet becomes its own teacher: the original sentence is the answer key.

(A) If the answer were shown first, there would be nothing to learn. The guess comes first, and the real word checks it.

(C) Self-supervision means the labels come from the text itself, not from people.

options.optionText: The model sees the answer before each guess
The hidden word is already in the text, so the text checks each guess
Humans label a few examples, and the model copies them
